title: Leveraging Large Language Model to Generate a Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm with CRISPE Framework
authors: Rui Zhong, Yuefeng Xu, Chao Zhang, Jun Yu
text:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is an advanced AI technique that can generate text, images, music, or other media with similar structures to the training data [1,2]. As the generative adversarial network (GAN) [3] and transformer [4] were reported in 2014 and 2017, respectively, the rapid development of generative AI has attracted widespread attention from scholars. Especially in recent years, large model generative AI models have sprung up like mushrooms, such as Bing Chat [5], LLaMA [6,7], DALL-E [8,9], ChatGPT series [10,11,12,13], and Gemini [14]. These large language models (LLMs) have been widely applied and achieved great success in art, writing, education, product design, medicine, gaming, marketing, and other fields [15,16,17,18].

Evolutionary computation (EC), a sub-field of AI and soft computing, is a family of population-based stochastic optimization techniques inspired by natural phenomena or organism behaviors. A general flowchart of EC techniques is demonstrated in Figure 1, encompassing five primary steps: (1). Initialization, which involves setting up the population and parameters, (2). Offspring generation, (3). Evaluation, (4). Selection, and (5). Iteration of step (2) to step (4) until the process reaches termination. Within these steps, the design of specialized search operators in step (2) stands as the core element of the EC technique, which can be realized by imitating the social behaviors of animals [19,20,21] or by simulating the laws of science [22,23,24]. Thanks to its scalability, easy implementation, robustness, and applicability, this approach has become one of the most favored optimization methodologies in both academic fields and real-world applications [25,26].

Additionally, the existence of the No Free Lunch Theorem (NFLT) [27] suggests that the performance of any given metaheuristic algorithm (MA) cannot be guaranteed across all possible optimization problems. This uncertainty has sparked a surge in the development of the novel MAs. Therefore, the motivation of this research is to design a novel MA by integrating the LLM with the CRISPE framework.

In this paper, we propose an LLM-assisted MA named the zoological search optimization (ZSO) algorithm. This innovative algorithm draws inspiration from the collective behavior and adaptation strategies observed in various animal species. It uniquely combines the concepts of social communication, dynamic collaboration, and individual adaptability to offer a unique metaheuristic approach for tackling black-box optimization problems. In the meantime, we address a critical limitation in the field of EC, as highlighted in [28]: the inadequate experimental validation often associated with newly proposed MAs. Thus, we implement a set of numerical experiments to investigate the performance of the proposed ZSO comprehensively. Moreover, we manually design four hyperparameter adaptation strategies and embed them into the ZSO. Experimental results and statistical analysis provide a practical verification of the high competitiveness of the proposed ZSO when compared to other expert-designed MAs. The specific contributions of this paper are outlined as follows:

- • Through the CRISPE framework and ChatGPT-3.5, we propose a novel zoological search optimization (ZSO) algorithm, specifically tailored for continuous optimization.

- • We comprehensively investigate the performance of ZSO in CEC2014 benchmark functions, CEC2022 benchmark functions, and six engineering problems. 20 popular MAs are employed as competitors.

- • We introduce four hyperparameter adaptation variations within the ZSO framework.

- • Both experimental and statistical results confirm the efficiency and robustness of the ZSO in various scenarios.

- • This research also explores the future trajectory of the metaheuristics community in the era of the LLM.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 involves the related works including the recent development of LLM-assisted EC techniques and an overview of the CRISPE framework. Section 3 covers a detailed introduction to the methodology in this study. Section 4 presents the numerical experiments conducted, along with the statistical results obtained from these optimization tests. Section 5 analyzes the performance of the proposed ZSO and provides some potential topics for EC promotion leveraging the LLM technique. Finally, Section 6 concludes the key findings and insights.
